articles.title_orig: Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
articles.title_zh: Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
articles.content_orig:
Watch as fire engulfs Hitler's mountaintop retreat
Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a 33-year-old German man during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.
Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 local time (19:15 GMT) on Friday and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.
Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to the scene where the blaze was still burning early on Saturday, as police said difficult terrain hindered efforts to bring the fire under control.
Police said they apprehended the suspect riding a motorcycle near the scene and possible motives were still being examined, German media reported. A criminal investigation has been launched.
There is currently nothing to suggest the involvement of further suspects, police official Gerhart Holzinger told a press conference on Saturday afternoon.
Public prosecutor Rainer Vietze said a psychiatric report had concluded the 33-year-old man showed signs of possible mental illness and diminished responsibility might therefore be assumed.
Vietze said a possible political motive was also being considered, but stressed the investigation was in its early stages.
The residence, above the town of Berchtesgaden, was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.
Hitler and top Nazi officials used his nearby Berghof residence to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941 and the whole complex was considered one of his headquarters.
He also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.
Local media reported that site had been "largely destroyed" and the public was urged to avoid the area.
Bavaria's Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann told reporters that the site would "under no circumstances remain a ruin", broadcaster BR24 reported. "It is important that we continue our work of remembrance," he added.
The retreat was seen smouldering on Saturday morning
Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest, which sits at an elevation of around 1,800m (5,900ft), escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945.
Since then, it has become a popular tourist destination and houses a mountain inn.
It serves as "a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship", according to its official website , external .
During WW2, Hitler and his followers were responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people, including the mass murder of European Jews. Homosexuals, gypsies, the disabled and ethnic minorities were sent to concentration camps and put to death.
There has been a wider debate in Germany and Vienna over whether to preserve, repurpose or demolish buildings connected to Hitler.
While some say these buildings should be preserved for historical reasons, others have raised concerns that they could be used as monuments or places of pilgrimage for neo-Nazis and far-right extremists.
In June, Berlin authorities announced they would tear down one of Hitler's bunkers - described at the time as "the power centre of Nazi Germany" - to build flats and offices on the site.
Those critical of the plans said the bunker had "significant historical value" and that it should have been turned into a museum and memorial site with an exhibit about the end of the war.
And in July, after years of controversy, Austrian authorities refurbished the house in the town of Braunau am Inn in which Hitler was born and turned it into a police station.

articles.title_orig: France deploys 70,000 police to try to contain nationwide protests
articles.title_zh: France deploys 70,000 police to try to contain nationwide protests
articles.content_orig:
French police have arrested dozens and fired tear gas at some protestors Saturday as authorities stepped up security in major cities, aiming to prevent a repeat of last week's rioting . The nationwide demonstrations are focused on the high cost of living, and a massive turnout is expected again after more than half a million took to the streets last week.
France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 135 people have been arrested and a variety of weapons have been seized. The items confiscated include metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said. Nuñez added that, so far, "there has been no major incident" in the country.
Nuñez previously said as many as 70,000 officers will be deployed nationwide, along with helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.
Demonstrations had been banned in the southeast city of Lyon, but about 150 protesters near the city's center briefly tried to block a road. Police fired tear gas to disperse the group. Tear gas was also used to break up a group of around 1,000 people gathered in the south of the city.
A police helicopter was seen flying over the city, and security forces, armored vehicles and riot police vans were patrolling. A 21-year-old student, who spoke to the Agence France-Presse on the condition of anonymity, described authorities as "really mobile."
In the western city of Nantes, thousands of protesters broke through police lines to enter the city center, the AFP reported. Officers used tear gas and a water cannon to try and disperse them. Some on the fringes of the demonstration threw projectiles and aimed fireworks at officers.
Police used tear gas in several cities, including Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand, and Strasbourg, and water cannons in Nice and Nantes, French media reported. In Marseille, officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march's endpoint.
In Orleans, thousands of people marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party. Le Pen is launching her campaign to succeed Emmanuel Macron as France's president. Elections will be held in six months, and surveys show Le Pen is best-placed to win. Demonstrators in Orleans protested both Macron and Le Pen.
"Macron resign. Le Pen in prison," the crowd yelled, according to the AFP. Police put their numbers at 11,000, while organizers said 26,000 took part. About 50 organizations, including labor unions, left-wing parties and student groups, had called for a protest against Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party.
French media reported that the protest against the congress ended peacefully early Saturday afternoon. The gathering is expected to continue through Sunday.
Authorities described the atmosphere in Paris as "calm" as hundreds gathered at the Porte d'Italie for the city's only authorized march. The gathering was set to be held at the Bastille, in the city's center, but police ordered it moved to the more remote location on Paris' southeastern rim at the last minute.
Union organizers said they reluctantly agreed to the change. But union representative Murielle Guilbert told reporters that it was "scandalous" that Macron had forbidden protestors from demonstrating "where we wish to demonstrate."
"We are here today, quite obviously, because there is immense social anger in this country, and because wages have still not been increased to the level they should be," she added.
The front of the march ended without incident. Some chanted "We are not happy" as they peeled away from the Porte de Vincennes. Police say 110,000 people took part in the march.
More than 3,000 were stopped and checked by officers, police said. The Paris prosecutor's office said 64 people had been arrested and 40 placed in police custody, including six minors. Most arrests concerned suspected weapons offenses or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage, the office said.
A student named Lucas told CBS Saturday Morning that he believed it was "normal for people to be angry."
"There's like an escalation because people, we think that the government is not listening," Lucas said.
Throughout Paris, major museums are closed and many businesses have been boarded up. Art Basel, one of the world's most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.
The first-ever NFL game in France between the New Orleans Saints and the Pittsburgh Steelers remains scheduled for Paris on Sunday, but some associated venues have been shuttered. A pop-up NFL shop and the "NFL House," where the Super Bowl trophy is on display and community sessions and events were scheduled, were closed Saturday. A similar venue for the New Orleans Saints was also postponed until Sunday. Another NFL pop-up shop remains open in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, the league said. NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said earlier this week that preparations for the game had been made in consultation with U.S. and French authorities.
A soccer game scheduled to be held in Paris on Sunday, between Paris Saint-Germain and Olympique Lyonnais, has been postponed until Monday night.
Parisian shopkeepers have been barricading their stores all week. Near Place de la République in Paris, one of last weekend's hot spots, a bank branch and other businesses were boarded up with wooden panels to deter potential looters.
Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted last weekend. The demonstrations first erupted last month when high school students in the southeast of Paris protested for better conditions, but quickly spread across the country as people took to the streets to demand relief from rising living costs.
One group of protesters, the Yellow Vests, said they would hold another round of protests on Oct. 31. The Yellow Vests emerged about eight years ago as a loosely organized group that staged disruptive protests against Macron.
Organizers called for rallies and a sit-in outside parliament and city halls nationwide, condemning the "authoritarian drift" of Macron's government and urging citizens to stand up for "public freedoms."
Other protests are expected across Europe on Saturday, encompassing a broad range of issues including pensions, housing costs, anti-war movements, education and corruption.
Italy deployed soldiers to Milan, the nation's fashion and finance capital, as the city braced for fresh demonstrations one week after looting and police clashes. Many stores were boarded up with wooden planks on Saturday. Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters.
In Rome, authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up patrols around key sites. Several hundred students demonstrated peacefully in the historic city. Organizers of peaceful events sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and their hands visible.
In Albania's capital of Tirana, riot police used water cannons to subdue large groups of protesters. Some of the demonstrators threw projectiles at police, the AP reported. A separate protest organized by the opposition outside the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama turned violent earlier Saturday, with some activists lighting fires on the street. The demonstrators are mainly high school and university students, demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. A broader anti-government movement is calling for Rama's resignation.
In Spain, thousands of retirees and others marched through central Madrid to demand that public pensions aren't meddled with.
Protestors in Lisbon, Portugal, are expected to march across the city Saturday to demand affordable housing.
AFP

articles.title_orig: What to expect from Apple’s ‘Pro and tell’ event
articles.title_zh: What to expect from Apple’s ‘Pro and tell’ event
articles.content_orig:
Apple’s long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro, an OLED iPad Mini, and more.
Apple’s long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro, an OLED iPad Mini, and more.
It feels like Apple’s Welcome Home event just happened. And the iPhone Duo announcement isn’t all that far in our rearview mirror, either. Yet, the company is back with another launch, focused on the MacBook Pro, it looks like. Its “ Pro and tell ” event is scheduled for October 28th at 1PM ET in Los Angeles. While obviously nothing is confirmed yet, it sure seems like we’re finally going to get that long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro.
Beyond that? There could be an OLED update for the iPad Mini, plus M6 updates across other devices, following the M6 debut with the Mac Mini in August.
A MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen has been a fixture of the rumor mill since at least early 2023 . But now, in late 2026, it may finally come to fruition. The name MacBook Ultra has been floating around, but Apple is unlikely to rebrand its flagship laptop line.
This will be the first touchscreen laptop and the first OLED laptop from Apple. It will supposedly feature an iPhone-esque Dynamic Island, but don’t expect a dramatic revamp of the macOS interface — The touchscreen MacBook isn’t going to be some sort of iPad hybrid . It may include a few flourishes, like a magnification effect when you touch the screen or new gesture controls in native apps. But that’s it.
It’s also going to stick with the M5 series of chips for the time being — specifically, the M5 Pro and M5 Max. There might not be an M6 Pro or Max , even. Instead, Apple may wait to upgrade its higher-end processors until it introduces the M7 next year .
That doesn’t mean there won’t be an M6 MacBook Pro, however. The base model of the MacBook Pro could be getting a bump from the M5 after the M6 debuted in the Mac Mini earlier this year. It might also get a slight redesign, including a hole-punch style camera. Unfortunately, they’re also expected to come with a price increase as component shortages reverberate through the Apple lineup.
The iMac is also expected to get an M6 update, nearly two years after its last revision. Apple’s all-in-one desktop appears like it’s going to skip right over the M5. Don’t expect any real changes beyond that, though. But at least we might get some new color options, just like we did with the M4 model.
Another long-rumored device that might finally be making its debut on Wednesday is the OLED iPad Mini . Other than the iPad Pro, the tablet lineup has stuck with LCDs until now. The new OLED iPad could kick off a broader transition for the product line. The screen upgrade may add $100 to the cost, though. Otherwise, it likely won’t be a significant redesign, but expect a processor upgrade from the aging A17 to the A20 that debuted with the iPhone 18.

articles.title_orig: China urges US to halt proposed expansion of outbound investment curbs
articles.title_zh: China urges US to halt proposed expansion of outbound investment curbs
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Treasury Department is moving to restrict American investment in China’s life sciences industry, releasing long-anticipated proposed rules that add biotechnology to the Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security (COINS) Act.
Published Thursday, the draft regulations (PDF) categorize “pharmaceutical compounds” as a “prohibited technology” that would trigger an outright ban on certain outbound transactions with “countries of concern,” such as China. The definition of pharmaceutical compounds runs the gamut of different modalities, spanning small molecules, polymers, vaccines, blood products, allergenics, cell and gene therapies, monoclonal antibodies and other recombinant therapeutic proteins, as well as their delivery systems.
If implemented in its current form, the rules would cause additional headaches for U.S. biopharmas looking to tap into China’s biotech innovations. But despite the sweeping scope of the ban covering various types of drug molecules, biopharma business development teams can breathe a measured sigh of relief.
The proposed rule largely spares the regular in-licensing deals and fee-for-service drug R&D collaborations that have driven the majority of multi-billion-dollar deals between Western biopharma companies and their Chinese counterparts. This detail fits the description of a Reuters report in September, which said the Treasury was working on rules that would continue to allow pharma companies to strike most licensing deals for Chinese drugs.
In an accompanying Q&A (PDF), the Treasury Department outlined the types of investment that would be covered under its rules: “Under the proposed rule, certain transactions that involve the acquisition of equity, provision of debt financing that is convertible to equity or that carries certain rights, greenfield investments or other corporate expansions, the creation of joint ventures, or certain LP investments would be covered.
“Activities that do not meet the definition of a covered national security transaction would not be subject to the program except where they are undertaken to evade or avoid the proposed rule,” the agency explained.
Therefore, traditional asset licensing agreements, where Western drugmakers pay cash, milestones and sales royalties for ex-China rights to drugs, fall outside the scope of covered transactions.
The language of the rules matches the current text of the COINS Act itself. COINS was enacted as part of the fiscal year 2026 national defense bill, giving the Treasury the power to scrutinize—or outright prohibit—American investments in sensitive foreign sectors involving countries it views as adversaries. While the law does not name biotech, it allows Treasury to add new sectors when devising specific rules.
When calls for including biotechnology in the COINS Act emerged earlier this year, Laurie Burlingame, a lawyer at Morse, Barnes-Brown & Pendleton, who specializes in life sciences transactions, explained to Fierce that a pure sectoral expansion of the law likely wouldn’t cover pharma licensing deals, as the law is highly focused on equity investments rather than usual product transactions.
Several high-profile U.S. Big Pharma deals with Chinese companies have drawn scrutiny from Washington’s China hawks in their COINS Act expansion push. But those transactions appear to be pure licensing agreements based on public announcements. These include Bristol Myers Squibb’s potential $15.2 billion deal with Hengrui Pharma covering 13 early-stage programs.
However, some other transaction types that have gained traction lately would fall victim to the rules.
The COINS Act lists “acquisition of an equity interest” in a Chinese entity as a “covered national security transaction.” This provision would prevent U.S. venture capital firms from investing in Chinese biotechs, and it would also impact future deals resembling Pfizer’s recent partnership with 3SBio.
When Pfizer in-licensed a PD-1xVEGF bispecific antibody from 3SBio last year, the New York pharma made a $100 million equity investment in the Chinese biotech. That deal structure would be prohibited under the proposed Treasury rules.
Burlingame previously raised concerns over the COINS Act’s potential impact on the “NewCo” model, in which venture capitalists form a new U.S. biotech based on assets licensed from China. The Chinese licensor often takes an equity stake in the new firm to capture long-term upside.
Under existing COINS language, only Chinese ownership of 50% or above would make the NewCo a target as a Chinese entity. But the proposed Treasury rules’ anti-evasion clause could subject any future China deals that involve an equity interest component to additional scrutiny.
In addition, “entrance into a joint venture” also marks a notable transaction category regulated by the COINS Act.
In its proposed rules, the Treasury deliberately chose not to define “joint venture,” instead, it “refers to the plain English meaning of the term, i.e., as involving the contribution of capital and/or assets by two parties and the sharing of profits and losses.”
This murky definition adds uncertainties to some deals. In Pfizer’s $10.5 billion , 12-asset collaboration with Innovent Biologics, the two companies will co-develop four programs globally and share the development costs, plus U.S. and European profits or losses. Although this unincorporated partnership doesn’t necessarily fit the common idea of a joint venture business, it does involve the contribution of capital from both parties to fund R&D and profit-sharing, and the Treasury said that its term “would not require the establishment or formation of a new entity.”
It’s not immediately clear if the Treasury means to crack down on this deal structure. If it does, the Pfizer-Innovent accord could face regulatory actions—only transactions completed before the enactment of the COINS Act on Dec. 18, 2025, are exempt from the Treasury rules, if implemented.
Following the release of the draft rules, the biopharma industry has reacted with a cautious tone, warning against any broadly restrictive provisions as they study the policy’s details.
“The Administration is correct that biotechnology is a strategic technology industry for the United States. We need policies and initiatives that maintain and advance our global leadership in biotech, particularly as we compete with China,” John Crowley, president and CEO of the influential biotech industry lobby group Biotechnology Innovation Organization (BIO), said in a statement Thursday.
“The details of the proposed Treasury Department rules matter. We cannot restrict our way to success,” he continued. “As Treasury considers comments on the proposed rule, we need to ensure that we do not have an overly broad approach that would create uncertainty for innovators and investors and that may unintentionally risk weakening U.S. biotech competitiveness.”
In a separate statement, Kendalle Burlin O’Connell, CEO and president of Massachusetts biotech trade association MassBio, said that “efforts to address national security risks must be carefully targeted to avoid undermining the innovation ecosystem that has made the United States a global leader in developing new medicines.”
“For Massachusetts’ biotech industry, international partnerships and licensing agreements can bring promising scientific discoveries into the U.S. drug development pipeline, where American companies invest in and advance potential new therapies,” she added. “Preserving the ability to develop breakthrough innovations from our own world-leading domestic pipeline while also identifying promising innovations from elsewhere is essential to maintaining America's competitive advantage and access for U.S. patients.”

articles.title_orig: Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start amid high chocolate prices and affordability concerns
articles.title_zh: Halloween candy sales are off to a slow start amid high chocolate prices and affordability concerns
articles.content_orig:

American households struggling with elevated living expenses and steep chocolate prices have driven a sluggish start to Halloween candy sales this year.
Figures from market research firm NielsenIQ reveal that candy purchases fell 6.7% in the month ending Oct. 17 compared to the same period last year.
An 11.7% drop in mid-September wiped out early-season sales gains recorded over the previous two years.
Chris Costagli, a vice president and food thought leader at NielsenIQ, said surging fuel costs have worsened concerns over affordability, curbing demand for treats.
As of Friday, the national average for regular gasoline stood at $4.29 a gallon, up nearly 40% from last year.
"I think what you’re seeing now is a consumer that’s spending so much additional money on fuel and housing and clothing and food," Costagli said.
"Some of the decisions they're making about Halloween candy, it’s not necessarily because, 'I notice it's more expensive than last year,' it's, ‘I can’t afford it this year because I've paid so much more for so many other things. I just don’t have the financial means to buy it this year.’"
Costagli noted that small bags were the only package size seeing sales growth through mid-October, while large and extra-large sizes experienced the sharpest declines.
U.S. candy prices have outpaced general inflation for several years.
Government data shows candy and gum prices jumped 44% over a five-year period through September, while overall grocery costs rose 22.5% over the same timeframe.
Discount grocer Aldi advertised a 135-piece variety pack of Mars Inc. chocolates—including Milky Way, Trix and Snickers—for $19.87 this week.
That is nearly the same price consumers paid for a 250-piece pack five years ago.
High cocoa prices are the primary driver. Global cocoa costs hit a record $10,710 per metric ton in January 2025 due to harsh weather in West Africa, which produces 70% of world supply, and speculative futures trading, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Although cocoa dropped to $3,241 per metric ton in March, prices rebounded in the spring after the Iran war disrupted fertilizer shipments to Africa.
The El Niño weather pattern is also expected to dampen output, bringing heat and dry conditions through February.
Costagli noted that demand remains weak even where prices have dropped. Non-chocolate treats like gummies and lollipops averaged $6.08 per pound in the nine weeks ending Oct. 17, down roughly 3% from last year, without driving a surge in sales.
Sally Lyons Wyatt, a global executive vice president and food industry adviser at Circana, said consumers are coping with high grocery bills by making smaller, more frequent shopping trips right before using items.
She questioned whether buyers are simply holding off until closer to Halloween.
"People are very intentional and thoughtful about what they want to consume, not just for holidays, but in general," she said. "I do believe we will still see softness overall with candy, but I don’t think Halloween is doomed."
The National Confectioners Association, representing producers such as Mars, Smarties Candy Co. and Ferrara Candy Co., said it remains optimistic.
"We are just now entering the peak period for Halloween and consumer enthusiasm remains incredibly strong," the group said Friday in a statement.

articles.title_orig: British police received allegations about Meghan’s father in 2019 but didn’t tell other forces
articles.title_zh: British police received allegations about Meghan’s father in 2019 but didn’t tell other forces
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Police in the British capital said Saturday that they received a letter containing allegations about the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, in 2019, but did not tell other law enforcement agencies.
Authorities in the Philippines confirmed this week that they are investigating Thomas Markle over claims that he kept child sexual abuse images at his home. He has denied the allegations.
Meghan said in a statement Friday that she was “deeply distressed” by the allegations and that she was previously informed by police of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018.
A spokesperson for London’s Metropolitan Police said a review of records confirmed that the force received a letter in January 2019 “containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.”
“It was sent to the MPS Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex,” the statement added. “The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.”
The statement did not say whether any investigation took place or if any further action was taken.
The force said it was reviewing the incident and considering whether to refer itself to the United Kingdom’s Independent Office for Police Conduct.
Asked about the discrepancy between the two statements on the date of the letter, a spokesperson for Meghan told NBC News she “may have been mistaken by a few months.”
The allegations against Thomas Markle were first reported Thursday by The Sun, a British tabloid, which reported that his son had informed police after he said he found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father’s home.
The Sun published a photo it said showed the son, Thomas Markle Jr., signing a sworn statement it said he had submitted to police and quoted him as saying: “I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.”
In a statement Friday, Meghan addressed the report that her father was being investigated.
“The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” said Meghan, whose relationship with her father has been limited and fraught in recent years. He did not attend her wedding to Prince Harry in 2018, drawing widespread media scrutiny.
She said the letter sent to the British police and other authorities in 2018 “made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.”
Meghan added that she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.”
The elder Markle, 82, denied the reported allegations, calling them “sick lies” in a statement to Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper. He added they were “the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”
His daughter Samantha Markle also dismissed her brother’s allegations, telling the Daily Mail that “there is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever. ... He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”
NBC News did not immediately receive responses to requests for comment from Markle Jr. or Samantha Markle — Meghan’s half-siblings.
NBC News was not immediately able to identify a contact for Markle Sr., who the Daily Mail reported was now in a Florida rehab center recovering from surgery.
In a statement, the FBI said it was “aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of U.S. law.”
The Philippines’ justice department confirmed Friday that “the matter is under investigation” but otherwise declined to “provide further details at this time.”
Meghan, 45, and Harry, 42, moved back to the United Kingdom earlier this summer after several years in the United States.
The couple last week made their first joint public appearance since returning to the U.K. , visiting charities in central England. King Charles III has made clear that their return does not signal a return to active royal life. Harry, however, has said recently that he wants his disagreements with his family to “work out.”
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_orig: In U.S. Gas Talks With Kremlin, Hidden Financing for Alaska Project Emerges
articles.title_zh: In U.S. Gas Talks With Kremlin, Hidden Financing for Alaska Project Emerges
articles.content_orig:
Almost the entire management team of the US$25 billion US gas project Polar Train LNG has left the company following allegations of undisclosed financing and control by Russia's Novatek.
Details : The Financial Times reported that the company's former chief executive, Joel Riddle, raised concerns about potential violations of US sanctions.
Polar Train LNG is developing a gas export terminal in northern Alaska. The project was launched in March with a plan to use a partially constructed Novatek terminal and relocate it to Alaska. The company applied to the US Treasury Department for permission to negotiate with the Russian group but has yet to receive approval.
Riddle said he discovered that Novatek was already financing the project and directing its operations before the necessary approvals had been obtained. He resigned in September, after which chief financial officer Dan Chandra and other executives also left the company.
"I resigned as chief executive of Polar LNG because I felt uncomfortable that the Russian company Novatek was financing and ultimately controlling the strategic direction of the company," said Riddle.
He initially believed that the funding was being provided by Gentry Beach, an investor with ties to Donald Trump's family, and Abu Dhabi-based company Tech Wave. Riddle said he later discovered that Beach had not invested in the project and was neither a shareholder nor an executive.
The FT also reviewed WhatsApp messages in which Novatek board member Denis Solovyov discussed financing the project and sought to expedite the transfer of funds to Polar Train LNG.
Polar LNG said Riddle had been dismissed, described him as a "disgruntled employee" and stressed that it was developing the project in compliance with US law.
Novatek said it had agreed to grant Tech Wave the right to use its technology in Alaska and had signed a memorandum with Polar Train in April, when Riddle was still running the company.
According to people who spoke to the FT, the project had featured in talks between Washington and Moscow over business deals that could help bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. The discussions included a potential exchange under which Novatek would provide its expertise for the construction of the Alaska terminal in return for sanctions being lifted on Russia's Arctic LNG 2 project.

articles.title_orig: Kim Jong-un Makes First Visit to China in Over a Year
articles.title_zh: Kim Jong-un Makes First Visit to China in Over a Year
articles.content_orig:
SEOUL, South Korea — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited China on Saturday, inaugurating a new bridge that connects the two countries and saying he hoped to expand cooperation with his powerful neighbor.
Kim’s visit to China is his latest move in an increasingly assertive foreign policy as he seeks to align Pyongyang with Beijing and Moscow in a united front against the United States under what he portrays as a “new Cold War.” It’s his first visit in a year.
Kim arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong Saturday after crossing the newly opened bridge, according to South Korea’s Unification Ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea, and China’s official Xinhua News Agency.
He met with Wang Huning, a member of the Standing Committee of China’s Communist Party. The two toured a car factory, and promised to strengthen the bilateral relationship.
Kim said his country “stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation, thereby delivering tangible benefits to the peoples of both countries,” Xinhua said.
Wang then accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, according to Xinhua. North Korean state media did not immediately report on Kim’s visit.
Experts said the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge this month was a key symbol of strengthening ties between North Korea and China and reflected their intent to expand trade, as it is expected to accommodate two-way traffic around the clock, including container shipments and heavy cargo trucks.
Kim has recently sought to strengthen ties with China, the North’s traditional main ally and economic lifeline, after years of prioritizing ties with Russia. He sent thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine, possibly in exchange for military and economic assistance.
Kim’s latest visit to China is his sixth since taking power in late 2011 following the death of his father. The visit appears to be timed to underscore the strength of his ties with Beijing ahead of the Oct. 25 anniversary of China’s first major victory in the Korean War, which was days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River into North Korea in October 1950.
The war began with North Korea’s surprise attack on the South in June 1950, prompting a U.N.-led coalition headed by the United States to intervene and push back the offensive. North Korea was backed primarily by Chinese forces, with assistance from the then-Soviet Union’s air force, before fighting ended with a 1953 armistice that left the peninsula technically at war.
Kim said his visit on Saturday was also to memorialize those killed in the war, according to Xinhua.
Chinese President Xi Jinping traveled to Pyongyang in June for a meeting with Kim. During their summit, Xi expressed Beijing’s willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority.
Kim last visited Beijing in September 2025, when he met with Xi and watched a military parade alongside Putin and other foreign leaders.
Kim has maintained a hard line toward Seoul and has so far rebuffed a proposal from U.S. President Donald Trump to revive their diplomacy, which broke down in 2019 during Trump’s first term. Kim’s government has called for Washington to abandon its “hostile policy” and drop demands for the North’s denuclearization as a precondition for renewed talks.
South Korea’s liberal government, which favors engagement with the North, hopes renewed talks between Washington and Pyongyang will thaw inter-Korean relations, and has also urged China to play a “constructive” role in resolving the standoff. Seoul’s spy agency told lawmakers last month that it saw a 50% possibility of a meeting between Trump and Kim on the sidelines of next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, or APEC, summit in Shenzhen, China.
“From Seoul’s perspective, if North Korea focuses more on economic development than military buildup and threats, that would be positive for diplomacy and security,” said Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
“But if Kim can extract ever more benefits from China and Russia, it is unclear what Seoul could offer that would be worth the political risks Pyongyang attaches to exchanges with a more prosperous, globalized, and free Korea.”

articles.title_orig: Is Iran planning attacks on Americans; why is the US on alert?
articles.title_zh: Is Iran planning attacks on Americans; why is the US on alert?
articles.content_orig:
United States intelligence agencies have warned that Iran is in “advanced stages” of plans to target US personnel abroad, prompting Washington to place staff on high alert in the Middle East, according to US officials and an official memo cited by Axios and The New York Times (NYT).
The alert comes as the US and Israel signal they may be preparing for a new military campaign against Iran, which Tehran has reportedly threatened to retaliate against, in part by targeting communications cables in the Gulf.
The heightened threat assessment has prompted Washington, already on guard over escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthis, to trim Washington’s diplomatic presence in the Middle East, the NYT has reported, citing officials.
Here’s what we know about the latest US warning, and how it fits into the broader US-Iran conflict:
A warning about Iranian plans to target US citizens was detailed in a memo sent by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, first reported by US news site Axios.
In the memo, Clayton wrote that US agencies had received intelligence indicating that Iran has “substantially increased efforts to target US personnel” overseas, with lethal plots reaching “advanced stages” in the Middle East and other countries.
The NYT, which also reported on the memo, cited unnamed US officials as saying threats to American officials, including ambassadors, had been assessed in recent weeks, and that Iran had lined up potential targets in Europe.
The officials said some intelligence indicates Iranian operatives are already active within the US.
Washington has not publicly commented on the memo, although the NYT cited a US official as confirming its authenticity on behalf of President Donald Trump’s administration.
Another official cited by the NYT played down Iran’s ability to execute attacks inside the US and elsewhere, saying it lacks the capacity to follow through on all its ambitions.
According to officials cited by the NYT, US agencies deem Iranian threats to US citizens in the Middle East to be “at the highest level” since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February.
This assessment is behind the US’s recent moves to withdraw staff posted in the region, the NYT added.
In the background are reported US and Israel plans to initiate a new military campaign against Iran following the US mid-term elections next month . On Friday, Trump said the US “may do another little epic fury”, using the codename for the US-Israel war against Iran that began on February 28.
On Wednesday, the US Department of State announced it was removing non-essential staff in its embassy in Saudi Arabia, citing escalating attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen against Saudi infrastructure.
Staff levels have also been quietly reduced at other US diplomatic missions in the region, several US media have reported. That includes embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Lebanon, according to CNN.
A US official cited by the NYT said the threat of Houthi attacks and “Iranian terror plots targeting US officials” were driving US staffing decisions.
Iran has not responded to news of the US intelligence memo accusing it of planning attacks on US personnel.
However, Iranian officials have repeatedly threatened and carried out attacks against US bases and those of its allies in the region. The Pentagon has confirmed that 21 US military personnel have been killed in the Middle East since the war on Iran began.
On Wednesday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned that Tehran would follow a new “offensive” strategy if the US renewed attacks.
That means Tehran would no longer limit its military operations to retaliatory strikes, said IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi, adding that the quality, range and power of Iranian missiles had improved.
Tehran also has in-depth plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf in the event of new US-Israeli attacks, the Reuters news agency reported, citing two senior Iranian security officials.
Previously, Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence facilities across the region could come under attack if war with the US breaks out again.
Yes, US authorities have long accused Iran of being behind plots targeting US citizens, including assassination attempts against Trump on US soil.
In March this year, a Pakistani national was convicted by a US court of plotting to assassinate Trump and other US politicians on the orders of Iran’s IRGC.
An Iranian IRGC member was charged in 2022 with trying to assassinate former US National Security Advisor John Bolton. The individual allegedly “attempted to pay individuals in the United States $300,000 to carry out the murder in Washington DC or Maryland”, according to the US Department of Justice.
Last year, the US intelligence community warned that Iran would “continue to directly threaten US persons globally”, specifically targeting officials it believed were involved in the 2020 assassination of IRGC Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani .
This month, the US abruptly withdrew bombers from an airbase in England, United Kingdom, citing concerns about a potential attack. That followed a security incident at the base, after which the UK arrested several men on suspicion of working with Iranian intelligence.

articles.title_orig: Attention, Passengers: High Airfares May Be Here to Stay
articles.title_zh: Attention, Passengers: High Airfares May Be Here to Stay
articles.content_orig:
Fewer people are flying this year, but with airfare this high and climbing , airline executives say that's just fine.
At the New York Hilton in Midtown Manhattan on Friday night, the aviation industry held its annual Wings Club gala, honoring Ed Bastian, CEO of profit-leader Delta Air Lines .
North American airline CEOs and other executives at the black-tie bash told CNBC that demand trends aren't worrying them, but persistently high, profit-crimping fuel prices are.
The number of people screened at U.S. checkpoints is on track for its first annual decline since 2020. Major U.S. carriers have said capturing higher fares matters more than fully filling planes or flying record numbers of travelers.
"We're actively prioritizing yield versus load factor and really happy as we see it. It fits right in with the premium investments that we're making," American Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper said on the company's earnings call Thursday.
American's load factor, a gauge of how full planes are flying, fell to 83.4% in the third quarter from 86% in the same quarter of 2025.
Plane ticket prices have skyrocketed as airlines grapple with a spike in jet fuel prices, their biggest expense after labor, and pass more of those costs on to customers.
Fares in September were up more than 22% from a year earlier, according to the latest inflation read. Fare tracker Hopper said it expects this holiday season to come with the most expensive ticket prices in years.
The average Southwest Airlines fare in the third quarter, for example, was $231.69, up close to $50 from a year earlier. That doesn't include Southwest's new fees, like its extra charges for checked bags or a seat closer to the front of the plane.
The airline's revenue passenger count, however, fell 3.2% from a year ago to about 33.5 million people.
Still, both fares and the passenger counts exceeded Southwest's expectations.
"Passenger fares came in about $3 above what our forecast was and the more important thing is that passenger volumes also exceeded our expectations," Southwest CEO Bob Jordan said on an earnings call Thursday.
Since April — when airlines began warning in earnest about profits taking a hit from the spike in jet fuel — through Thursday, about 9.3 million fewer people were screened at airport checkpoints than in the same period of 2025, according to the Transportation Security Administration. That's down less than 2% from last year, but it follows years of growth.
With jet fuel prices more than double year-ago levels — as seen in U.S. Gulf Coast spot prices at $4.63 a gallon, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration — airlines have focused on recovering as much of the fuel spike as possible.
Despite some drops, airline executives said during their earnings calls that overall travel demand is robust, especially for profitable premium cabins like business class.
And not every carrier is seeing a decline. United Airlines flew 2.4% more passengers in the third quarter than a year ago and said its unit revenue rose 16%, the biggest increase since the pandemic.
"I've been pleasantly surprised at the industry's ability this year to raise yields and pass through much of the increase in fuel prices," CEO Scott Kirby said on the company's earnings call Wednesday. "So it's possible that airlines will continue to focus on yields at the expense of load factor and that alone could get us to double-digit margins next year."
Most airlines expect fuel costs to keep biting, but executives say they're confident in their pricing power.
United, for example, said it expects to pay an average of $4.80 per gallon for fuel in the fourth quarter, up from $3.90 per gallon in the third.
American, United, Delta and Southwest all cut their 2026 profit forecasts this month when they reported earnings. American is the only one of the four that expects to post a loss this year.
American and others have also reduced growth plans or warned the industry could dial back its capacity expansion goals, which could keep fares elevated. Reduced capacity can make bookable seats scarcer, driving up prices even more if demand holds.
The carriers said demand has been particularly strong for premium seats, which command hundreds, if not thousands of dollars, more than coach tickets.
"Today, we find ourselves yet at another inflection point for our industry and the world. ... Geopolitics affecting our business, driving the price of jet fuel to historic highs," Bastian said in his award-acceptance speech, adding that artificial intelligence makes it hard to predict months or weeks ahead.
"It causes many people to question yet again the durability of our industry. But I'm not worried because I know the people in this room, and I know your resilience and how you've demonstrated that time and time again," he said.
Smaller airlines set to report results in the coming weeks, starting with JetBlue Airways next week, followed by Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air , have traditionally focused on more price-sensitive customers, which could show if those travelers are pulling back at all.
One factor that could also affect air travel is the demise of Spirit Airlines, which went out of business in early May.
"Some of its customers have likely stopped flying," Bank of America said in a research note Thursday.
Many of the problems that plagued the airline industry for years are starting to abate.
In some cases, aircraft deliveries are still years behind schedule. But Boeing , whose CEO, Kelly Ortberg, attended on Friday night, and its main rival, Airbus, have ramped up production. Boeing will update investors on its production outlook when it reports quarterly results Tuesday.
The Federal Aviation Administration has approved Boeing's Max 7, a key smaller jet for Southwest Airlines, and the Max 10, which Alaska Airlines and United Airlines have been waiting for for years.
Pratt & Whitney parent, RTX , and GE Aerospace say they're improving engine durability and shop visit turnaround time, though customers say more improvements are needed.

articles.title_orig: WATCH: 200-foot office tower imploded in seconds in metro Atlanta
articles.title_zh: WATCH: 200-foot office tower imploded in seconds in metro Atlanta
articles.content_orig:
CHAMBLEE, Ga.  — A towering office building that stood for 45 years is now a pile of rubble after a planned implosion in Chamblee.
[DOWNLOAD: Free WSB-TV News app for alerts as news breaks ]
The 18-story glass tower on Century Boulevard came crashing down in a matter of seconds as crews set off explosives to bring the more than 200-foot-tall building to the ground.
Dave Savignano, owner of Cartersville-based Atlas Demolition, told Channel 2’s Bryan Mims that it takes extensive engineering to place explosive charges strategically and time the detonations.
“And within two seconds, the building should be safely on the ground,” he said. “It usually takes two to three seconds.”
NewsChopper 2 captured the implosion from above, showing the building collapse inward as smoke and dust filled the surrounding area.
The demolition came after a proposed $91 million plan to convert the building into 289 apartments was abandoned because the project was deemed unfeasible.
Highwoods Properties, which owns the building, could not find a new use for the aging structure.
Built in 1981, the tower previously housed the U.S. Department of Revenue until 2024.
The building’s triangular shape presented an additional challenge for engineers preparing for the implosion. The plan was to bring the structure down on itself, with the collapse expected to take about two seconds.
The Chamblee demolition brought back memories of another major Atlanta-area implosion: the Georgia Dome in 2017 .
The stadium, which opened in 1992, was once the second-largest covered stadium in the world. It hosted the Atlanta Falcons, Georgia State Panthers, two Super Bowls and Olympic events.
The Georgia Dome was also the only American stadium to host the Summer Olympics, a Super Bowl and the NCAA men’s basketball Final Four.
Its implosion cleared the way for Mercedes-Benz Stadium, which now stands next door.
The Chamblee office tower’s demolition marks the end of another chapter for a longtime fixture on the metro Atlanta skyline.

articles.title_orig: Apple Store Pickup System for iPhone Duo Just Went Live Again in U.S. and Canada
articles.title_zh: Apple Store Pickup System for iPhone Duo Just Went Live Again in U.S. and Canada
articles.content_orig:
The option to reserve an iPhone Duo for Apple Store pickup resumed in the U.S. and Canada between 5:10 a.m. and 5:15 a.m. Pacific Time today, but inventory is extremely limited, with most stores having no pickup slots available today.
You can search for iPhone Duo availability at your local Apple Stores by heading to the iPhone Duo order page , selecting your desired color and storage and so forth, and then opening the link next to the "Pickup" option at the bottom. Next, enter your ZIP code and you will be able to see if any models are available for pickup with a reserved time slot.
Apple Store pickup was offered for just a few minutes after iPhone Duo pre-orders began on Friday, October 16, and the option then disappeared until now.
The pickup system has also resumed in Australia, the U.K., Germany, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, Singapore, Japan, China, and some other countries.
Just hours after iPhone Duo pre-orders began last week, Apple said demand for the device was " nothing short of extraordinary ," with delivery estimates pushing into late January, so it is not surprising that Apple Store pickup slots are hard to come by right now. Apple said it is working to satisfy demand "as quickly as possible."
Given the scarcity, long queues formed at many Apple Stores around the world on Friday, with some lucky customers managing to secure an iPhone Duo on a walk-in basis. If you are still looking for an iPhone Duo, check Apple's pickup tool often.

articles.title_orig: The PHP Meltdown Shows How AI Makes Bugs More Exploitable
articles.title_zh: The PHP Meltdown Shows How AI Makes Bugs More Exploitable
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.
On Wednesday, a decades-old open-source web technology called PHP almost broke the internet, thanks to two vulnerabilities that had sat dormant for years until researchers recently figured out a way to exploit them.
The bugs are dubbed PHP2Shell , officially designated as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 . In simple terms, the bugs allow anyone who knows how to exploit them to break into an online system running PHP, such as a website or internet-facing server, without needing a password to access or modify its data.
As situations go, this was a pretty sizable one, forcing millions of people around the world to scramble to patch their systems before malicious hackers could abuse them.
The PHP Foundation, which maintains the PHP web software, publicly released patches on Wednesday that fixed the bugs, which when installed prevent web-facing servers from being attacked. The foundation had already given some of the biggest internet companies and web hosts that rely on PHP an early headstart on patching.
Thanks to weeks of backroom chatter and careful coordination across the industry, the world — so far — broadly avoided mass internet exploitation. From Wednesday, governments began urging citizens and companies with websites to take action to mitigate the risks on their ends. A wide range of industries shuttered their websites and pulled services offline to patch their systems. Banks, retailers, gaming sites, online stores, hospitals, and some government agencies took down their servers to prevent attacks.
But security researchers are warning that the situation isn’t over yet, and that a large number of systems around the world remain unpatched and vulnerable to hacks and data theft.
This is also unlikely to be the last major internet software scare, with some expecting the advent of AI to rapidly uncover as-yet-undiscovered vulnerabilities that are waiting to be found and abused.
Security researchers at Calif found two bugs in PHP, a programming language widely used around the world for building websites and web apps, both on the internet and hosted locally on company networks, like intranets and internal sites.
PHP is open-source, meaning it’s free and available to be used by anyone for almost any reason. As such, it’s become one of the most popular and broadly used web programming languages on the web today.
The two bugs were first discovered in 2024 but weren’t considered exploitable at the time, and weren’t patched. Security researchers recently found a way to exploit them, prompting them to alert the makers of the software to get them fixed.
Calif alerted the PHP Foundation, which began a period of fixing the bugs and coordinated disclosure. The foundation did this by offering the information and patches about the security issues under a tightly guarded embargo — essentially held confidentially until a specific deadline — to give big companies an opportunity to get ahead of installing the fixes.
PHP2Shell is pretty serious because it can be abused remotely over the internet and without the victim having to click on a link or open a file. This is known as remote code execution , and it’s one of the more damaging kinds of bugs to exploit because they can grant a hacker anywhere in the world effectively full control over an affected and unpatched system.
Worse, these specific PHP bugs make it possible to break into any unpatched system on the internet without needing a password or any other credential over the internet, known as unauthenticated access.
This would allow a malicious hacker to then plant malware on the computer, such as to steal data or simply to maintain a long-term foothold that they can return to later.
The bugs are particularly risky because PHP is wildly popular software, in part because it’s free and relatively easy to use, but also because it’s been around for decades. Around 70% of the web-facing internet relies on PHP, though its usage has been slowly declining over the years in favor of newer, more secure programming languages.
Given its popularity, some of the world’s most popular websites are run on web software that rely on PHP, such as WordPress (which hosts TechCrunch!), as well as Drupal, Joomla, and MediaWiki, which powers online encyclopedia giant Wikipedia.
PHP is just one of many aging but functional technologies that have survived waves of the internet and generations that are now so ubiquitous, they’re akin to the glue that holds much of the internet together. Oftentimes these tools are developed by open source maintainers, who are not paid for the work that they do, and as such cannot afford third-party security reviews — but are still widely relied on by companies who do not contribute financially to the projects.
Security researchers at Calif were credited with discovering the bugs earlier this year as part of a security audit of PHP’s code. Calif was participating in the Hack the Planet initiative by AI model maker OpenAI and cloud security giant Wiz, which subsequently verified the proof-of-concept exploits that Calif made.
In Calif’s write-up (featuring comics — it’s great, check it out ), the researchers explained that AI was used in assistance with exploiting the bug, but that the bulk of the work relied on knowledge that the researchers already had, and that they knew PHP’s codebase and exploitation history well.
“No model is simply capable of unearthing ‘all bugs’ with simple prompts. At least for now,”wrote Calif.
Despite efforts to keep details of the bugs under wraps until Wednesday, it does appear that there was some PHP2Shell exploitation prior to the release of patches.
Amazon, which has enormous visibility into online threats due to its size and scale, said in a blog post that it detected exploitation of PHP2Shell about a week before the PHP patches were available, suggesting that someone, somewhere, knew how to exploit the bugs before their details were broadly available. Amazon said it wasn’t clear how the hacker learned of the vulnerabilities, but that defenders should look for evidence of exploitation as early as October 17.
There are a few theories as to what happened. Once a bug is patched, the details of the patch can become immediately apparent, especially if the code — like in PHP’s case — is open source, making it public and inspectable. Exploiting the bugs might not be easy, but knowing where the bug is and how it was fixed can allow malicious hackers to understand where to target and how to develop their exploits.
It’s possible that there was a leak or a breakdown in communication somewhere during the embargo. The open source community is enormous and controlling information in this fashion relies on good-faith.
It’s also possible that hackers discovered the bugs ahead of time, either independently or through espionage.
The PHP Foundation blamed one company for pushing the patches live hours before the embargo period was up, which could have given some attackers a headstart if they obtained details of the patch before others. But this doesn’t account for the week-long activity detected by Amazon.
Researchers say that bugs require a lot of work to become exploitable and weaponizing the bug has been a challenge — but not impossible — which explains why we haven’t seen a scale of mass-exploitation just yet.
But as of late Friday, there are now confirmed compromises and post-exploit activity related to the PHP bug, according to security giants Palo Alto Networks and Trail of Bits . That means the bug was detected being abused to hack in and actively do malicious activity on an as-yet-unknown target.
It’s still early days but it’s an encouraging sign that there haven’t been any signs of mass-exploitation — but we’re not out of the danger-zone just yet.
Matthew Prince, the chief executive of network security and monitoring giant

articles.title_orig: Engadget Review Recap: iPhone Duo, Rivian R2 And More
articles.title_zh: Engadget Review Recap: iPhone Duo, Rivian R2 And More
articles.content_orig:
A roundup of recent reviews from Engadget.
We've reached the point of the tech calendar where the pace of new devices is just absurd. Over the last two weeks, the team here at Engadget has published over a dozen reviews. That in-depth testing runs the gamut from Switch 2 controllers to repairable laptops and a new Alexa tablet to unique wireless microphones . I can't fit all of them in this roundup, so be sure to check out our reviews hub after you read up on the biggest recently tested products below.
There's no doubt the iPhone Duo was one of the most-anticipated devices of the year. Surprisingly, Apple's first attempt at a folding phone doesn't seem like a first-generation device. Yes, it's heavy and expensive, and many apps still need to be optimized for its interior screen, but there's a lot to like here if you can afford one.
"The company had the luxury to learn from its competitors' accomplishments and missteps, which means the iPhone Duo has sidestepped most of the growing pains a new class of gadget might normally encounter," senior reviews reporter Sam Rutherford said.
Before he set off folding the latest iPhone, Sam spent some time behind the wheel of the mid-sized Rivian R2 . He discovered a roomy SUV with great power and range, and an interior that checks all the boxes. There's fine-tuning to still be done, and you might want to wait for the base model to arrive next year.
"Rivian is proving that just because an electric SUV is smaller and more affordable, that doesn't mean it has to make major trade-offs to its style, power and tech compared to the rest of its siblings," he said. "For a family of four, the R2 feels like the Goldilocks SUV that could make people who currently drive gas-powered rivals jump to an EV and never look back.:
If you've ever wanted the benefits of a pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses without the creepy cameras, there's now a stylish, audio-only option in the Ray-Ban Meta Audio . The frame styles look more like "normal" glasses, they offer longer battery life due to the lack of cameras and, most importantly, they're comfortable to wear.
"One of my favorite things about the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses is just how 'normal' they look and feel," senior reporter Karissa Bell said. "I was still able to enjoy the open-ear speakers and other audio features without being constantly aware that I was wearing smart glasses, or that others around me might notice them."
Technics impressed us in 2025 with its AZ100 true wireless earbuds and now the company has put its magnetic fluid driver tech in a set of over-ear headphones. With the A1000 , the company offers excellent sound quality and ANC performance alongside a comfy design and solid battery life. The two problems? They cost $450 and one of the standout features is unreliable.
"The true wireless AZ100 made a big impression, thanks in part to those Magnetic Fluid drivers, and the A1000 builds on that success with equally impressive sound," contributing reviews writer James Trew said. "Truly, they're a joy to wear and to listen to."
Senior reviews reporter Devindra Hardawar spent the last week testing the first laptop he could get his hands on with NVIDIA's new RTX Spark chip inside: the ASUS ProArt P16 . He discovered an expensive yet extremely powerful laptop that really isn't meant to be used by most of us.
"The ASUS ProArt P16 is an impressive premium laptop, undoubtedly. But its high starting cost and unique hardware make it something that's truly only tempting for AI professionals," he said. "I'd give the entire RTX Spark platform at least a year before I could recommend it to general users or even gamers."

Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 149, your guide to the best and Verge -iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, happy It Actually Feels Like Fall Now At Least In My Neighborhood), and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage .)
This week, I’ve been reading about Demis Hassabis and computer chips and permafrost , enjoying the first episodes of Machine Gods ,filming the next season of Version History (pet season!), seeing You Can See Everything and then reading and listening to absolutely everything about it, painstakingly updating all the stuff in my 1Password , making tiny documents with Tiny Little Office , watching Conan O’Brien own Subway Takes the way he once owned Hot Ones ,finally getting properly good at CapCut , and blasting the soundtrack to The Mandalorian and Grogu all workday long.
I also have for you a new AI assistant, the most Duo-y new app for the iPhone Duo, my hunt for the next great browser, and much more. Let’s do this.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What are you playing / reading / watching / listening to / modding with Claude this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com . And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer , forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here .)
The worst news of the week here in the Installerverse is that Arc is going away . This was obviously coming: The Browser Company bailed on Arc two years ago in favor of the more AI-centric Dia, and Arc has been in maintenance mode ever since. But now it’s not just being ignored, it’s going away. By Christmas, you won’t even be able to use the app anymore.
So now a lot of us are stuck looking for another browser. There are a million new ones out there, many of them somewhere between “heavily inspired by Arc” and “a direct copy of Arc I made in Codex this morning.” I need to test a lot of them. I don’t know exactly where I’ll land yet, but I figured I’d share a bunch of the ones I’m looking at:
On mobile, it’s easy. Quiche is my favorite iOS browser by a mile. Arc was never great on Android, so I’m betting most of us never switched there in the first place.
There are also the default browsers, of course, like Chrome, Safari, and Edge. But each of those browsers continues to fail me in one way or another, and so my search continues. If you’ve found your browser of the future, tell me all about it! Otherwise, I’ll report back here periodically through my journey.
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky .
“ Youth is an absolute SCREAM on HBO Max at the moment.” — Jonathan
“ Todoist has a stellar integration with Siri AI that has finally made me fully commit to just using it If you delete Reminders, Todoist becomes the default on Siri AI and you can add a to-do to any project with tag AND location support (using Apple Maps saved locations like home and work!). The best part is that it all works WITHOUT having to say ‘... in todoist’ at the end of each query!” — Sajishnu
“Apple added Sound Glow to existing HomePod models and it’s just kinda fun to watch the light on top of HomePod glow and flash. So I’m doing that with some of my favorite playlists.” — Connor
“I’m reading a book called How to Read a Book by Mortimer J. Adler because I want to get better at analysis and reading for understanding vs. absorbing basic information.” — Rhoades
“My girlfriend took a train ride up the west coast and reported that no less than four different people asked her if her 2024 Samsung Galaxy Z-Flip 6 was the new iPhone Duo.” — Nicholas
“I recently read Bodies of Magic by Freya Marske, and it was excellent. What if med school was magical, but everyone was still sleeping with each other and stressing over student loans? Then an unexpected dead body shows up during finals.” — Emmett
“I got a Framework Laptop 13 Pro running Ubuntu last month, and I’m really happy with it. (I haven’t done anything with Linux in maybe 20 years — it’s come a long way!) So now I’m trying to see if I can replace Capture One with Darktable . If I can, that would break my last tie to macOS, and I’ll replace my iMac with a Framework Desktop.” — Morgan
“Exploring the new Nektropos Castle dungeon in EverQuest Legends . The game has been such a nostalgia trip back to 1999, but new content in an ancient game is a bizarre delight.” — Alex
“Setting up Navidrome and having Claude build me a definitive ‘Songs From the Black Hole’ playlist from my Weezer MP3 collection. (It’s harder than first appears: is ‘Lisa’ track 12 or not!?)” — Micheal
“Best Buy had a pretty insane deal on a Bambu A1 Mini , so we got my 12 year old son a 3D printer for his birthday. It’s amazing how easy it was to put out a seemingly perfectly accurate PLA print, compared to horror stories from older printers.” — Jeff
Last week, my wife and I went car shopping. Our plan was just to drive a bunch of cars — we knew we needed something with three rows, and really had no experience with any of them — and then go home. Somehow, a few hours later, we were the proud and slightly bewildered owners of a new Kia Carnival .
So far the car has been great, but wow are there a lot of weird tech ideas in cars now. I’m good with CarPlay and Android Auto. I hate how much everything has become a touchscreen. But I’m most thrown by how many features of my car now exist in a companion app. How do we feel about this? I almost miss when I had no idea what to do about the check engine light.
Anyway, I’m a minivan dad now. I think I’m okay with it. Send car tips! Send minivan tips! Send help! See you next week!

WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Canadian jet maker Bombardier plans to invest $270 million in the United States and add 300 jobs, the company ‌said on Friday, days after President Donald Trump dropped threats to ban ‌the company from the country.
Trump's September threats against Bombardier became a political issue in Kansas, where ​the company employs 1,500 people in Wichita. The threatened ban prompted calls to the White House from Kansas lawmakers, including Republican Senator Roger Marshall, who is facing a tough race in the November 3 elections. In a speech in Wichita ‌on Monday, Trump said he ⁠did not plan to hurt Bombardier and would take care of its workers.
Bombardier announced $50 million of the investment in its Wichita ⁠operations earlier this month and plans additional funding for its operations in Indiana, Connecticut and Texas.
Bombardier reiterated on Friday it is hiring for 500 roles open across ​the US ​and said it is planning to create ​an additional 300 jobs through ‌expansion projects.
"Based on our constructive conversations with the US administration, we see a bright path forward for our highly skilled aerospace workers as well as a positive environment for Bombardier to continue pursuing direct investments to grow our American footprint," CEO Eric Martel said.
Bombardier shares were flat on Friday in midday trading.
In a ‌Truth Social post late on Thursday, Trump said ​Bombardier's investment would create jobs in Kansas, Texas, ​and Indiana.
Bombardier, which acquired Learjet ​and established its US headquarters in Kansas in 1990, has ‌3,500 employees in the US, more ​than 40% of whom ​are in Wichita.
In February, Trump had threatened to decertify Bombardier aircraft over a certification dispute involving rival Gulfstream Aerospace. That threat never materialized because ​Transport Canada ultimately approved ‌the jets.

articles.title_orig: I didn't believe this Claude wizardry could actually speed up my Google TV until I tried it
articles.title_zh: I didn't believe this Claude wizardry could actually speed up my Google TV until I tried it
articles.content_orig:
I have never really been a fan of Android TVs or low-end streaming boxes because they tend to slow down drastically over time.
I have multiple smart TVs at home running Android TV or Google TV, and all of them have become painfully slow. So when I saw a viral post on X about using Claude to speed up an old Android TV, I decided to give it a shot.
Surprisingly, everything worked, but what impressed me most was how little I had to do. Claude handled most of the setup and cleanup with minimal input from me.
Since I have dabbled with custom ROMs on Android phones in the past, I always knew I could debloat my old Android TVs to speed things up and free up internal storage. But I never bothered, as the process seemed convoluted and required more time than I could squeeze into my schedule.
Seeing other people do it on X with relative ease using Claude gave me a reason to try. I did not expect the process to be straightforward and seamless. It took a few minutes and required minimal input on my part.
Before trying this experiment on the old Android TV in my living room, I started with a Mi Box S connected to an old TV in my bedroom. It's running Android 9 with a September 2021 security patch. With only around 1GB of free space and limited RAM, the device had become painfully slow.
To get started, I enabled ADB on the Mi Box S from the hidden Developer Options menu . This streaming box doesn't support wireless ADB. But if you have a newer Android TV model, you'll also need to enable wireless ADB debugging in the Developer Options menu.
After that, I fired up a Claude Code instance on my Mac and gave it a simple prompt: "Find the Mi Box streaming box on my network. I have ADB enabled. Check if you can access it."
Claude took it from there. It first detected that I did not have ADB installed on my Mac. Then, it scanned my home network, found two Xiaomi devices, and checked both for an open ADB port. The initial scan didn't find one, but a second check located the Mi Box.
After that, Claude installed ADB through Homebrew on my Mac and attempted to connect to the Mi Box. I had to approve the "Allow USB debugging?" prompt on my TV. Claude then verified the connection and gathered more device information.
After Claude had access to my Mi Box S, I told it to debloat the box so that it would run more smoothly and faster. Instead of uninstalling everything immediately, Claude scanned the installed software and identified non-critical system packages.
Then it generated a list of bloatware it could uninstall to free up storage space and speed up the streaming box.
More importantly, it recommended a reversible method to remove these packages, leaving all OS, launcher, and Google framework packages untouched during the cleanup.
It even listed the preinstalled streaming apps and asked which ones I didn't use so it could uninstall them.
During the process, Claude suggested removing PatchWall, Xiaomi's Android TV launcher, because it would significantly boost speed. However, my Mi Box S would then default to the standard Android TV home screen.
While I liked the PatchWall experience, a smoother and faster Android TV experience was a bigger win for me. So this was an easy decision. Many users on X replaced the Google TV launcher with something lightweight, but I was okay with this trade-off.
Within a few minutes, Claude debloated the Mi Box S and removed unnecessary packages to free up storage and RAM. At the end, it asked whether I wanted to disable the background cache and animations for extra speed, though I decided against it.
The process felt surreal because it went so smoothly. I repeated it on other old Android and Google TVs in my house to make them faster.
What I liked was that Claude didn't just uninstall everything without my consent. Instead, it asked which apps I wanted to keep and which I didn't care about.
I had known for years that I could debloat my old Android TV or install a minimalistic launcher to make it faster. But because of the complexity, I never bothered to take the time. Claude closed that gap, handling the setup and cleanup with minimal input from me.
I still decided what to keep and remove, but I no longer had to figure out the commands myself. That convenience finally got me to tackle a job I had put off for years.
